settings.heading: What Is Sublimation Printing?
settings.answer: Sublimation printing uses heat to turn solid dye into gas that bonds inside polyester fibers, so the design becomes part of the fabric itself. It delivers permanent, full-color, zero-feel prints that won't crack or peel — but it only works on polyester-rich fabrics in white or light colors.

settings.text: Sublimation is a dye process, not an ink layer: at roughly 385–400°F the solid dye turns straight to gas, polyester's pores open, and the dye bonds inside the fiber. The print is in the fabric, not on it.
Polyester-rich fabric only — roughly 65%+ poly is the usual floor, and the higher the poly content, the more vibrant the result. On cotton the dye has nothing to bond to and washes out.
Sublimation dyes are transparent and there is no white ink — so blanks must be white or light-colored. Any white in your art is just the garment showing through.
Because the dye lives inside the fiber, the print has zero hand feel and won't crack, peel, or flake — it typically lasts as long as the garment itself.

The starter kit is small: a sublimation printer (a converted Epson EcoTank or a purpose-built Sawgrass), sublimation ink and paper, and a heat press run at about 385–400°F for 40–60 seconds. Entry cost is roughly $300–500.
Bayou stocks poly and performance blanks — athletic tees and jerseys by the pack from 99¢/unit. Stock is unbranded liquidation, so check each listing for fiber content before you sublimate.

settings.question: What is sublimation printing?
settings.answer: Sublimation printing is a decoration method where solid dye is turned directly into gas by heat and bonded into polyester fibers. The design is printed with sublimation ink onto special transfer paper, then heat-pressed onto the blank; the dye becomes part of the fabric rather than a layer sitting on top. The result is a permanent, full-color print with zero hand feel.

settings.question: How does sublimation printing work, step by step?
settings.answer: The design is printed mirrored onto sublimation paper using sublimation ink. The paper is placed face-down on the blank and pressed at roughly 385–400°F for 40–60 seconds. At that temperature the solid dye sublimates — turns straight to gas — while the heat opens the polyester's pores. The gaseous dye flows in and bonds with the polymer; when the press lifts and the fabric cools, the pores close and the dye is locked inside the fiber permanently.

settings.question: Does sublimation work on cotton?
settings.answer: No — sublimation dye bonds to polymers, and cotton has none, so the dye sits loose and washes out. Workarounds exist (poly coating sprays and sublimation-coated HTV that you press onto cotton first), but you're really sublimating onto an added poly layer, which changes the feel and durability. For cotton blanks, DTF or screen printing is the honest answer.

settings.question: Why do sublimation blanks have to be white or light-colored?
settings.answer: Sublimation dyes are transparent and there is no white sublimation ink, so the garment color shows through everything you print. On a white or light blank the colors read true and any white in your art is simply the fabric. On a dark blank the design effectively disappears. If you need to decorate darks, use DTF or HTV, which lay down opaque layers.

settings.question: How long does a sublimation print last?
settings.answer: Typically as long as the garment itself. Because the dye is bonded inside the fiber rather than layered on top, there is no film or ink layer to crack, peel, or flake off — the usual failure modes of other methods. Wash-for-wash it's the most permanent of the common decoration methods on the fabrics it works on.

settings.question: What do I need to start sublimation printing, and what does it cost?
settings.answer: Four things: a sublimation printer (crafters often convert an Epson EcoTank; purpose-built Sawgrass printers start around $600), sublimation ink, sublimation transfer paper, and a heat press that reliably holds 385–400°F. With a converted printer, entry cost runs roughly $300–500 all-in. The same setup also decorates poly-coated hard goods like mugs and tumblers.
